summary: Do not touch. All parts contain urushiol oil, which causes severe contact dermatitis in most people. Learn it first, before anything else on this list.
id_marks: Always exactly 3 leaflets; the middle leaflet has a noticeably longer stalk than the two side ones
Side leaflets are lopsided, usually with one coarse lobe or tooth on the outer edge only
Leaves alternate along the stem (never opposite pairs)
Glossy when new, often reddish new growth; grows as ground cover, shrub, or hairy climbing vine
White-ish waxy berries in late summer
cautions: Urushiol persists on tools, clothing, gloves and pet fur for months
NEVER burn it — inhaled smoke causes lung inflammation that can be life-threatening
Jewelweed, which often grows nearby, is the traditional field wash for exposure
lookalikes: Virginia creeper — 5 leaflets, harmless to touch
Box elder seedlings — 3 leaflets but OPPOSITE, not alternate
Raspberry/blackberry — 3-5 leaflets but with thorns and toothed all around

summary: One of the most useful and reliably identifiable roadside plants. Edible greens plus the classic field poultice for bites, stings and scrapes.

parts.prep: Raw in salad when small and tender; older leaves get stringy — steam or add to soup. Strip the tough parallel veins.
Chew or crush into a poultice for insect bites, stings, splinters and minor cuts — drawing/anti-itch action.
Strip the spikes, dry. Grind into flour extender or use whole — same family as psyllium, so a mild bulk fiber.

id_marks: Broad oval leaves in a flat basal rosette, no stem
3–7 heavy parallel veins running the length of the leaf; snap a leaf and the veins pull out like strings
Rat-tail seed spike rising straight from the center
cautions: Roadside plants absorb vehicle exhaust and road salt — harvest well back from pavement and away from sprayed lawns
lookalikes: Narrowleaf plantain (P. lanceolata) — same uses, skinnier leaves

summary: Entirely edible, every part, all season. There is no toxic lookalike that will hurt you in the dandelion group.

parts.season: Best before flowering; again after frost
parts.prep: Raw when young. Bitter once the plant flowers — boil in a change of water, or sauté with fat and acid.
Petals only (green base is bitter) into fritters, wine, or infused honey.
Roast and grind for a coffee substitute. Traditional bitter digestive and liver tonic.
Pick from the crown, sauté in butter — taste is close to artichoke heart.

id_marks: Basal rosette only — leaves never grow up a stem
Backward-pointing triangular teeth ('lion's tooth') along the leaf
Single flower head per hollow, leafless stalk; milky sap when broken
cautions: Avoid sprayed lawns and roadside verges
lookalikes: Cat's ear and hawkweed — hairy leaves, branched stems; harmless but blander

summary: Edible flowers and leaves, best known as a sweet tea. Eat in moderation rather than in bulk.

parts.prep: Pick fresh pink heads (skip browning ones). Dry for tea, or pull individual florets into salad — they taste faintly of honey.
Best cooked. Raw clover in quantity is hard to digest.

id_marks: Three leaflets, each with a pale V-shaped chevron
Dense round-to-oval pink-magenta flower head sitting right on a pair of leaves
Softly hairy stems
cautions: Contains phytoestrogens — those with hormone-sensitive conditions or on blood thinners should be cautious
Do not use moldy or brown/fermenting flower heads (coumarol / anticoagulant risk)
lookalikes: White clover — also edible, same rules

summary: Edible in small amounts, cooked for preference. Everywhere underfoot.

parts.prep: Dried for tea, or dipped and fried. Sweet.
Boil or steam briefly; raw clover in quantity causes bloating.

id_marks: Creeping stems that root as they go
Three leaflets, usually with a pale watermark
White-to-pinkish ball-shaped flower head on a bare stalk
cautions: Eat modestly — not a bulk green
lookalikes: Wood sorrel (Oxalis) — also 3 parts but heart-shaped leaflets and sour taste; edible but oxalic

summary: Classic wound herb — 'nosebleed plant.' Culinary use is as a strong bitter herb, not a vegetable.

parts.prep: Crushed as a styptic poultice to slow bleeding on minor cuts; also a bitter tea for colds/fever.
Very pungent — use like a bitter herb, a pinch at a time, not as a green.

id_marks: Feathery, finely dissected fern-like leaves — 'thousand leaf'
Strong sweet-medicinal smell when crushed
Flat-topped cluster of small white (sometimes pink) flowers
cautions: Do not use during pregnancy
Can cause photosensitivity and skin rash in sensitive people
Ragweed-family allergy sufferers may react
lookalikes: Poison hemlock and water hemlock also have dissected leaves — but yarrow's leaves are feathery-fuzzy and aromatic; hemlocks are smooth, hairless and foul-smelling with purple-blotched stems. Never confuse these.

summary: Genuinely edible — it is the wild ancestor of the carrot — but it lives in the one plant family that can kill you outright. Only harvest if you can positively rule out poison hemlock and water hemlock, every single time.

parts.season: Fall of year one / spring of year two
parts.prep: Only from a plant with no flower stalk yet. Pale, woody-cored, strongly carrot-scented. Cook it.
Battered and fried, or steeped into a delicate jelly/syrup.
Dry and use as a spice — flavor much like caraway.

id_marks: Stems are HAIRY — 'the Queen has hairy legs.' This is the key test.
Flat white umbel with a ring of feathery, forked bracts beneath it
Usually a single tiny dark purple floret in the center of the umbel
Whole plant smells distinctly of carrot
Umbel curls up into a 'bird's nest' as it goes to seed
cautions: POISON HEMLOCK (Conium maculatum): hairless stems with purple/red blotches, musty smell — FATAL
WATER HEMLOCK (Cicuta maculata): the most toxic plant in North America, wet ground, chambered root — FATAL
WILD PARSNIP and giant hogweed sap cause severe burning blisters in sunlight
If the stem is smooth or blotched, walk away. No exceptions.
Avoid during pregnancy — seeds have a traditional contraceptive/abortifacient use
lookalikes: Poison hemlock
Water hemlock
Wild parsnip
Yarrow (harmless)

summary: Pleasant anise-tinged tea herb. Note: it does NOT cause hay fever — its pollen is heavy and insect-carried. Ragweed, blooming at the same time, is the real culprit.

parts.prep: Dry the flowering tops for tea. Fresh flowers make a golden infused honey or can be battered and fried.
Cooked as a potherb; mildly bitter.
Traditional urinary/kidney tonic tea and an anti-inflammatory.
Yields a strong yellow-gold natural dye for wool.

id_marks: Tall unbranched stem with alternate lance-shaped, toothed leaves
Dense one-sided plume of tiny golden flowers at the top
Leaves get smaller as they go up the stem
cautions: Asteraceae-family allergy sufferers should test cautiously
Do not confuse with ragweed growing alongside it
lookalikes: Common ragweed — greenish spike-like flowers, deeply cut leaves; not useful as food

summary: The actual cause of late-summer hay fever. Not a forage plant — worth knowing purely so you can blame the right species and avoid it.
id_marks: Deeply dissected, fern-like leaves, often opposite low on the plant
Greenish, unshowy flower spikes at the tips — no petals
Disturbed ground, gravel shoulders, field edges
cautions: Major allergen — a single plant releases enormous quantities of wind-borne pollen
Handling can irritate skin in sensitive people
lookalikes: Mugwort
Young yarrow — but yarrow's leaves are far finer and aromatic

summary: The single most useful field remedy on this list — the standard wash for poison ivy exposure, and it conveniently grows in the same damp ground.

parts.prep: Crush the succulent stem and rub the juice on skin after poison ivy or nettle contact, or on bug bites. Can be simmered and frozen into cubes for later.
Pop the ripe pods into a bag — the seed inside tastes remarkably like walnut. Tiny but excellent trail nibble.
Historically boiled in two changes of water. High in calcium oxalate — genuinely not worth the risk as a vegetable.

id_marks: Translucent, watery, almost succulent stems with swollen nodes
Orange, spotted, horn-shaped flowers dangling on thread-like stalks
Ripe seed pods explode at a touch — hence 'touch-me-not'
Water beads up silver on the leaf underside
Damp shady ground, streamsides, ditches
cautions: Do not eat the greens in quantity — oxalate content
Pale yellow jewelweed (I. pallida) works identically
lookalikes: None dangerous

summary: A mint-family herb with a long medicinal reputation and no dangerous lookalikes. Mild enough to eat.

parts.prep: Raw in salad, or cooked. Slightly bitter, faintly minty.
Dried for a throat-soothing tea; traditional gargle for sore throat and a wash for minor wounds.

id_marks: Square stem (roll it between your fingers)
Opposite leaves
Blunt club-shaped flower head of hooded violet flowers stacked in tiers
Low sprawling growth in lawns, paths and grass
cautions: Mild; no significant toxicity known
lookalikes: Other mints — all in this family are safe to taste-test

summary: Well-known medicinal, not a food. Its serious drug interactions are the reason to treat it with respect.

parts.prep: Infused in oil (turns deep red) for a topical nerve/bruise/burn oil; tinctured or dried for the traditional mood remedy.

id_marks: Five yellow petals, often with tiny black dots along the petal edges
Bushy spray of many stamens in the flower center
Hold a leaf to the light — it is covered in translucent 'perforations' (oil glands). This is the confirming test.
Opposite, stalkless leaves on a two-ridged stem
cautions: Causes photosensitivity — sunburn risk in people and grazing animals
Interacts with a long list of medications: antidepressants, birth control, blood thinners, immunosuppressants, some HIV and cancer drugs. Check before internal use.
lookalikes: Other Hypericum species — similar, weaker

summary: Not a food plant. Traditional external medicinal use and a good pollinator/dye plant.

parts.prep: Native American use as a wash for sores, snakebite and earache. Not for casual internal use.
Yields yellow-to-olive dye.

id_marks: Bristly-hairy stems and leaves
Golden-orange rays around a dark chocolate-brown domed center
Alternate, coarse, lance-shaped leaves
cautions: Considered mildly toxic if eaten in quantity
Can irritate skin in sensitive people
lookalikes: Coneflowers, sunflowers — none dangerous

summary: Ubiquitous roadside daisy. Historically a medicinal, not a vegetable.

parts.prep: Dried tea used traditionally as an astringent/diuretic and for bleeding. Also the old use as a strewn insect-repellent — hence 'fleabane.'

id_marks: Many very narrow white-to-pale-pink rays — far more numerous and thinner than a true daisy's
Small yellow center
Hairy, branching stems, often waist-high
cautions: Asteraceae allergies
Not recommended as a food green
lookalikes: Asters — bloom later in the fall

summary: A famous old cough remedy that modern evidence has retired. It contains liver-damaging alkaloids — treat as a plant to recognize, not to use.

parts.prep: Formerly smoked or brewed for coughs. Now advised against.

id_marks: Large hoof-shaped (colt's foot) leaves, angular-toothed, white-woolly underneath
Leaves appear only AFTER the flowers are gone — 'son before the father'
Dandelion-like yellow flowers in very early spring on scaly stalks
Dense colonies on gravel, roadsides, disturbed streambanks
cautions: Contains pyrrolizidine alkaloids — cumulative liver toxicity, banned or restricted in several countries
Do not use during pregnancy, while nursing, or in children
lookalikes: Butterbur (Petasites) — larger, similar alkaloid concerns

summary: The iconic Maine roadside lupine. Beautiful, and the seeds are poisonous — do not treat these as wild beans.
id_marks: Palmate leaves — 9–17 leaflets radiating from one point like a wheel spoke
Tall dense spike of pea-shaped flowers (purple/blue/pink), followed by hairy pods
Water beads spectacularly in the center of the leaf
cautions: Seeds and pods contain quinolizidine alkaloids — toxic to people and livestock
Edible 'lupini beans' are a different, cultivated species and still require days of leaching
Do not eat any part of wild lupine
lookalikes: Vetches and other legumes — many also inedible

summary: Common scrambling roadside legume. Some species are toxic and species-level ID is difficult — treat the whole group as not-food.
id_marks: Pinnately compound leaves ending in a curling tendril
Small purple/violet pea flowers, often in a one-sided row
Scrambles over grasses and shrubs
cautions: Vicia seeds can contain toxic amino acids; hairy vetch has poisoned livestock
Grass pea relatives cause lathyrism (permanent paralysis) with sustained consumption
Do not eat
lookalikes: Groundnut (Apios americana) — a genuinely prime edible tuber with similar entire leaflets, but NO tendrils and a twining stem. Worth learning to separate.

summary: Every rose produces edible petals and vitamin-C-rich hips. No toxic lookalikes in the genus.

parts.prep: Best sweetened by frost. Split and scrape out the irritating inner hairs and seeds, then use for jelly, syrup, or tea. Very high in vitamin C.
Trim the bitter white heel. Use in syrup, jelly, sugar, or scattered on food.
Dried for a mild tea.

id_marks: Pinnately compound leaves, usually 5–9 toothed leaflets
Thorny/prickly canes
Leafy stipules fused to the base of the leaf stalk
Five-petaled pink or white flowers; orange-red hips after
cautions: The hairs inside the hip are a mechanical irritant — always strain or scrape them out
Multiflora rose is an invasive here; harvesting it freely is a public service
lookalikes: Raspberry/blackberry canes — also edible

summary: The safest wild fruit in North America — there is no poisonous lookalike for an aggregate berry on a thorny bramble cane.

parts.prep: Eat fresh. Raspberries pull free hollow, leaving the core on the plant; blackberries keep their core.
Use fully fresh OR fully dried — never wilting, which can produce mild toxins. Raspberry leaf is the classic uterine tonic tea.
Peel the first-year canes while tender and eat raw.

id_marks: Arching thorny canes
Compound leaves in 3s or 5s, sharply toothed, often silvery-white underneath (raspberry)
Aggregate fruit made of many tiny druplets
cautions: Avoid wilted leaves for tea
Nothing else — this one is genuinely beginner-safe
lookalikes: None dangerous

summary: Bright orange berry clusters. Edible cooked and after frost — genuinely unpleasant and mildly problematic raw.

parts.prep: Must be cooked, and much better after freezing. Classic use is a tart jelly served with game. High in vitamin C.
Traditional astringent tonic.

id_marks: Pinnately compound leaves with 11–17 narrow, sharply toothed leaflets
Flat clusters of white flowers, then dense orange-red berry clusters
Small tree of clearings and forest edges
cautions: Raw berries contain parasorbic acid — causes stomach upset. Cooking and freezing convert it to harmless sorbic acid.
Do not eat raw in quantity
lookalikes: Not a true ash — despite the name. Ash trees have OPPOSITE leaves; mountain-ash is alternate.

summary: A fine vitamin-C tea tree. Completely unrelated to poison hemlock the herb — the shared name has caused real confusion, but this conifer is safe.

parts.season: Best in spring when tips are bright green; usable year-round
parts.prep: Steep (don't hard boil) for a citrusy, vitamin-C-rich tea. The historic scurvy remedy in the north woods.
Dried and ground as a flour extender. Kills the tree if girdled — emergency only.
Very high tannin — the historic leather-tanning bark of Maine.

id_marks: Short flat needles ~1/2 inch, arranged in flat sprays, with two white stripes underneath
Needles attach by tiny stalks and leave bumpy pegs when pulled
Small delicate cones under an inch, hanging at branch tips
Feathery drooping leader at the treetop
cautions: Not related to poison hemlock (Conium) — different kingdom of problem entirely, but know the difference
Avoid strong conifer teas during pregnancy as a general precaution
lookalikes: Balsam fir and spruce — also safe for tea; yew (Taxus) is TOXIC and has flat needles too, but yew bears a red fleshy berry-like cone and no white stripes underneath

summary: Not food in any real sense, but a genuinely useful medicinal and survival tree — the source of natural salicin, aspirin's precursor.

parts.prep: Contains salicin — a traditional pain and fever tea. Also edible as a survival flour extender.
Resinous buds infused in oil make the traditional 'balm of Gilead' salve (strongest in balsam poplar).
Punky dry aspen is excellent friction-fire and tinder material.

id_marks: Nearly round leaves with a flattened stalk, which makes them tremble in any breeze
Big irregular teeth (bigtooth) or fine teeth (quaking)
Smooth pale greenish-white bark, dark and furrowed at the base of old trees
Grows in dense clonal stands from root suckers
cautions: Salicin is aspirin-like — avoid if allergic to aspirin, on blood thinners, or for children with fever (Reye's syndrome risk)
lookalikes: Birch — also salicin-bearing and useful

summary: Shrub dogwoods are a wildlife food, not a human one. Worth knowing for the leaf-vein trick, which is one of the most reliable ID tests in the woods.

parts.prep: Historically a bitter tonic, quinine substitute.
Strong, straight withes for basketry and skewers.

id_marks: Opposite leaves with strongly arcuate (curving) veins that follow the leaf edge toward the tip
Tear a leaf slowly — fine white latex strings stretch across the break. This is the confirming test.
Often red or reddish stems in winter; white or blue-white berries
cautions: Berries are bitter and can cause stomach upset — leave them for the birds
lookalikes: Invasive honeysuckle — also opposite leaves, but no arcuate veins and no latex strings

summary: An aggressive invasive shrub throughout this area. The tempting red berries are not edible — this is the classic 'looks like it should be food' trap.
id_marks: Opposite, simple, untoothed oval leaves, softly hairy
Older stems are HOLLOW — snap one and look. Native honeysuckles have solid pith.
Paired red or orange berries hanging on a shared stalk
Leafs out earlier in spring than almost everything else — the giveaway from a distance
cautions: Berries cause vomiting and diarrhea in quantity; not a food
Do not confuse with edible honeyberry/haskap (a cultivated Lonicera)
lookalikes: Native bush-honeysuckle (Diervilla) — toothed leaves, yellow flowers
Dogwood — arcuate veins

summary: Harmless to touch — this is the vine you learn so you can stop panicking about it — but the berries are genuinely poisonous.
id_marks: FIVE leaflets radiating palmately from one point ('five leaves, let it be')
Coarsely toothed leaflets; brilliant scarlet in fall
Climbs by tendrils tipped with adhesive pads
Blue-black berries on bright red-pink stalks
cautions: Berries contain concentrated oxalate crystals — genuinely toxic, dangerous to children
Sap causes skin irritation in some people
Grows tangled with poison ivy constantly — count the leaflets before grabbing anything
lookalikes: Poison ivy — 3 leaflets, not 5. This is the single most useful distinction to learn.

summary: The classic root-beer root of the northern woods. The root is the useful part; the berries are not.

parts.prep: Long aromatic runners just under the leaf litter. Simmer for a spicy root-beer-flavored tea or small-batch soda. A traditional trail stimulant.
Cooked, in small quantity.

id_marks: A single long bare stalk from the ground splits into exactly 3 branches, each with 3–5 toothed leaflets, held in one flat horizontal plane
No visible woody stem — the 'leaf' is the whole plant above ground
Greenish-white flower balls hide UNDER the leaf canopy, on a separate short stalk
cautions: Dark purple berries: not considered edible, reportedly cause nausea
Harvesting the rhizome kills that plant — take sparingly from large colonies
lookalikes: Young ash saplings — but ash has OPPOSITE compound leaves on a woody stem
Bristly sarsaparilla (A. hispida) — bristly lower stem, avoid

summary: Small evergreen woodland herb, another traditional root-beer flavoring. Slow-growing — admire more than harvest.

parts.prep: A traditional root beer and soft-drink flavoring; also brewed as a medicinal tea for the urinary tract.

id_marks: Whorls of glossy, dark green, leathery, sharply toothed leaves, widest above the middle
Only 4–10 inches tall, evergreen, in dry pine/oak duff
Nodding waxy pink-white flowers in summer
cautions: Contains hydroquinone-type compounds — not for regular or long-term internal use, or in pregnancy
Slow to spread and locally uncommon — harvest little or nothing
lookalikes: Spotted wintergreen (C. maculata) — white-striped veins
Teaberry/wintergreen (Gaultheria) — alternate leaves, strong wintergreen smell, edible red berries

summary: A bristly mint-family weed of Maine field edges. Not a stinging nettle, and not a useful green.

parts.prep: Old European folk use as a respiratory tea. Little modern support; not recommended.

id_marks: Square stem, distinctly SWOLLEN just below each leaf node — the key feature
Stiff downward-pointing bristles on the stem
Whorls of small pink-purple hooded flowers with a spiny calyx, stacked at the leaf joints
cautions: Bristles irritate skin
Not worth eating
lookalikes: Stinging nettle (Urtica dioica) — a genuinely excellent cooked green; it has narrower, more deeply toothed leaves, stings sharply on contact, and no swollen nodes

summary: Invasive mat-forming roadside plant. Its close relative cleavers is the useful one; this species is mostly a nuisance with minor uses.

parts.prep: Cooked; bland and slightly scratchy. The related cleavers (G. aparine) is the better spring tonic green.
Madder-family roots give a red-pink dye.
The historic mattress stuffing — hence 'bedstraw.'

id_marks: Whorls of 6–8 narrow leaves at each node, like spokes
Square, weak, sprawling stems forming dense mats
Airy clouds of tiny 4-petaled white flowers
cautions: Aggressive invasive in Maine hayfields
Some people get contact dermatitis from Galium
lookalikes: Cleavers (G. aparine) — sticky/velcro-textured, the preferred edible and lymphatic tonic

summary: Small cousin of fireweed. Edible in the same ways but far less rewarding.

parts.prep: Cooked like a green; bitter as it matures.
Dried, or fermented in the Russian 'Ivan chai' style (best with true fireweed).

id_marks: Four notched pink petals
A long, thin seed capsule below the flower that looks like a stalk — the family giveaway
Seeds released in silky white fluff
cautions: Mild; identify to genus and prefer true fireweed (Chamerion angustifolium) for actual use
lookalikes: Fireweed — much taller, showy magenta spikes, a genuinely good edible

summary: Edible when young, unpleasantly bitter once it bolts. The milky sap has a mild sedative reputation.

parts.prep: Raw when small; boil in a change of water once bitterness sets in.
Dried latex used historically as a mild sedative/pain reliever — 'lettuce opium.' Weak and unreliable.

id_marks: Deeply pinnately lobed leaves clasping a tall stem
Milky white sap from any break
A row of prickles along the underside midrib in prickly lettuce
Small dandelion-like yellow flowers, many per plant
cautions: Very bitter with age
Large amounts of the sap can cause nausea and drowsiness
lookalikes: Sow thistle — also edible
Dandelion — related, all safe in this group

summary: Do not eat. Fresh buttercup blisters skin and mouth — a common and easily avoided mistake among lawn greens.
id_marks: Palmately divided leaves cut into sharp, deep lobes
Glossy, almost lacquered-looking five-petaled yellow flowers
Common in damp pasture and lawn
cautions: Contains protoanemonin — causes blistering of skin and mucous membranes, and stomach inflammation if eaten
Toxicity breaks down on thorough drying (which is why hay is safe) but never rely on that
lookalikes: Marsh marigold — also requires cooking and is often misidentified
Wild geranium and cinquefoil — similar leaf shapes

summary: Toxic to eat, but one of the best wild cordage fibers in North America.

parts.season: Late fall–winter, after the plant dies back
parts.prep: Split the dry stalk, peel off the outer bark fiber, buff and reverse-wrap into exceptionally strong string.

id_marks: Opposite, untoothed, oval leaves
Reddish stems that branch in a forking pattern
Milky sap when broken
Long slender paired seed pods
cautions: Contains cardiac glycosides — genuinely poisonous, affects the heart. Do not eat any part.
Milky sap irritates skin and eyes
lookalikes: Common milkweed — larger, broader leaves, edible when properly cooked. Confusing the two is a classic and serious beginner error; milkweed pods are fat and warty, dogbane pods are thin as a bean.

summary: Evergreen woodland fern — useful as a winter green marker, not as food.

parts.prep: Stays green through winter — historically cut for Christmas decoration, and useful as emergency bedding insulation.

id_marks: Once-pinnate, leathery, dark green fronds — stays green all winter
Each leaflet has a small thumb/ear at its base, so it looks like a Christmas stocking
Silvery, scaly fiddleheads in spring
cautions: Not edible — do not confuse with ostrich fern fiddleheads
lookalikes: Ostrich fern (Matteuccia) — the ONLY commonly eaten fiddlehead in Maine: deep U-shaped grooved stem, papery brown scales, grows in floodplain clumps

summary: Important to know precisely because it grows alongside edible ostrich fern in the same wet ground.
id_marks: Broadly triangular frond with wavy-edged, nearly untoothed leaflets joined by a winged rachis
Dies at the first frost — hence 'sensitive'
Separate stiff, beaded, dark brown fertile stalks that persist all winter
cautions: Considered toxic — known to poison horses; fiddleheads are not safe to eat
Its fiddleheads emerge in the same wet ground as ostrich fern. Learn the difference before harvesting any fiddlehead.
lookalikes: Ostrich fern — the edible one. Check for the deep U-shaped groove down the stem and papery scales.

summary: The lacy fern that carpets Maine clearings in huge colonies. Smells like fresh hay when crushed. Not edible.
id_marks: Finely cut, lacy, yellow-green fronds, tapering at both ends
Sweet hay smell when crushed or when drying
Forms dense continuous colonies that shade out tree seedlings
cautions: Ferns in this family contain thiaminase and carcinogenic compounds — do not eat
Can cause contact dermatitis
lookalikes: Bracken fern — also inedible despite historic use

summary: Woody perennial bracket on conifers. Far too tough to eat, but a genuinely useful medicinal, tinder and dye fungus.

parts.prep: Chip or slice and simmer for a long time (an hour-plus) — a bitter, resinous tea with antimicrobial and anti-inflammatory traditional use.
The dried interior flesh takes a spark and holds a coal well; a good tinder/coal-carrier.
Yields yellow-brown to rust tones on wool.

id_marks: Hard, hoof- to shelf-shaped bracket on dead or dying conifers
Concentric zones: blackish-grey old center, a distinct RED-ORANGE resinous band, then a cream-white growing margin
The red crust looks like melted sealing wax — press a hot needle to it and it melts
Cream pore surface underneath that bruises yellowish
cautions: Too woody to eat — tea or extract only
Not a culinary mushroom; do not attempt to cook and eat the flesh
lookalikes: Hemlock varnish shelf / reishi (Ganoderma tsugae) — glossier, kidney-shaped, often stalked, softer when fresh; a better-known medicinal, also conifer-loving

summary: Old, algae-greened shelf fungi on a downed log. Too weathered to name with confidence — likely turkey tail or violet-toothed polypore.

parts.prep: Turkey tail is simmered for a well-studied immune-supportive tea. Only harvest fresh, flexible, clearly banded specimens — not weathered ones like these.

id_marks: Small thin overlapping shelves in tiers along dead wood
Turkey tail: velvety concentric bands of contrasting color, white pore surface with tiny pores
Violet-toothed polypore: purple-tinged, ragged tooth-like underside
cautions: Old weathered brackets are colonized by molds and algae — do not use
Confirm the underside before using anything called turkey tail: true turkey tail has fine pores, not a smooth surface (that would be the false turkey tail, Stereum)
lookalikes: False turkey tail (Stereum ostrea) — smooth underside, no pores

summary: An orange-brown capped mushroom in leaf litter. The underside was not photographed, so it cannot be identified — and unidentified mushrooms are not food.
id_marks: To identify a bolete you MUST photograph: the pore surface underneath, the stem (whole, dug not cut), a cut cross-section, and note any color change on bruising
Boletes have a sponge of pores under the cap rather than gills
cautions: Do not eat any mushroom identified only from a top-down photo
Most boletes are safe but several cause serious gastric illness, and red-pored, instantly blue-bruising species should always be avoided
Get a positive ID in hand from an experienced local forager or a Maine mycological society before ever eating a wild mushroom
lookalikes: Many — this genus needs in-hand examination

summary: Not a food tree, but one of the most valuable utility woods in the region — and one now under severe threat.

parts.prep: Splits along its growth rings, which is why brown ash is the traditional Wabanaki basket wood. Also the classic tool-handle and paddle wood.

id_marks: OPPOSITE compound leaves — one of the few trees here that does this
5–11 leaflets, pointed, finely toothed
Diamond-pattern furrowed bark on mature trunks
cautions: Emerald ash borer is killing ash across Maine — don't move ash firewood between areas
lookalikes: Wild sarsaparilla — herbaceous, single stalk splitting into 3
Mountain-ash — ALTERNATE leaves, unrelated

summary: Photos that are scene/habitat context, or where there isn't enough detail to name a single subject with confidence.
id_marks: For a confident ID later, capture: the whole plant, a close-up of a leaf showing arrangement (opposite vs alternate), the stem, the flower or fruit, and the growing habitat
cautions: Never eat anything from this category

summary: Common Milkweed is a stout native perennial of old fields and roadsides, recognizable by opposite oval leaves, milky sap, and warty teardrop-shaped pods. Several stages are traditionally eaten after boiling, but raw parts are bitter and mildly toxic, and confident ID plus proper cooking are both required. It is also the primary larval host for monarch butterflies, so harvest sparingly.

parts.prep: Boil in changes of water until tender; discard water. Never eat raw.
Boil until tender, serve like broccoli florets.

id_marks: Broken leaf or stem bleeds thick white latex sap
Leaves opposite, broad oval, entire, softly downy beneath with a stout pale midrib
Pods teardrop-shaped, covered in soft warty bumps, on a curved stalk
Stout unbranched stem, hairy, usually 3–5 ft tall
Fragrant dusty-pink flower umbels earlier in the season
cautions: Milky sap is irritating to eyes and skin — wash hands before touching your face
All parts contain cardiac glycosides; raw material can cause vomiting and heart effects, so boiling is mandatory
Leave most plants standing: this is a critical monarch host
lookalikes: Dogbane (Apocynum) — also has milky sap but slender branched reddish stems and thin dry paired seed pods, not warty ones; it is not edible
Swamp milkweed (A. incarnata) — narrow lance leaves and smooth slim pods
Butterfly weed (A. tuberosa) — orange flowers, alternate-ish leaves, watery sap

summary: A cup lichen: flat, scaly basal squamules on mossy bark or wood send up short stalks that flare into tiny grey-green goblets holding spores. Not a forage plant, but a good indicator of clean, humid, undisturbed woodland air. Several Cladonia species are nearly indistinguishable in the field without chemistry.
id_marks: Stalked podetia 5–15 mm tall, flaring abruptly into a shallow cup or trumpet
Pale grey-green to mineral-green surface, granular/mealy rather than glossy
Basal mat of small overlapping leafy scales (squamules), pale below
Growing over moss and bark on a trunk or log, not rooted in soil
Brittle and crisp when dry, softening and greening after rain
cautions: Lichens are not food — many contain bitter acids that irritate the gut; some Cladonia relatives are used in dyeing only
Extremely slow-growing; a handful pulled off is decades of growth. Photograph rather than collect
lookalikes: Cladonia chlorophaea group — cups with mealy interior; separating it from C. pyxidata requires spot tests
Cladonia fimbriata — more slender, evenly mealy stalks with narrower cups
Baeomyces or club-shaped Cladonia species — stalks tipped with a solid knob or pink disc, never a hollow cup
Small mushrooms — a true fungus has gills or pores under the cap; these cups are open on top with no gills
